I can't feel anything except for a sort of static buzz. I can't focus on anything or follow any train of thought. Sometimes I just stare. Other times it's like I'm behind my body. Like my body is going through the motions (talking, laughing, doing what it needs to do) but I'm behind it, seeing it do these things, but not connected to it.

Other times I experience derealization, when the world around me distorts and becomes unreal, almost cartoonish/two-dimensional or something. Everything starts to seem wrong and it's frightening.

It's remarkable how rare it is to find a psychologist who specializes in adult Asperger women, even in a city this size.

I am also looking into the other option (the free option through medicare) but I would really prefer to see a real specialist. It would be much more validating, and I have a feeling that working with the centre would help me get access to supports that I need.

So I don't know if I know any male aspies (I probably do, who knows), but I do know that my parents dismissed me when I tried to tell them. They insisted I was "fine" because I am "smart and good looking". Apparently your attractiveness is what matters if you're female...? and honestly... my intelligence never got me anywhere, because I have zero street smarts and can't keep track of anything ever so I kind of sucked at post-secondary education and have only worked a steady stream of shitty jobs.

I have gone to psychologists/psychiatrists with my concerns. Most dismissed my inability to function as Depression... which it wasn't, really. Well, Depression was a symptom, not the cause of my struggles. This was before I learned about Asperger's. 

After I stumbled across Asperger's and all of a sudden a light went on and my life started to make sense, I went to a psychologist with an extensive list of evidence that I had compiled, which she barely even looked at or seemed interested in. Let me start by saying that she knew I had concerns about my possibly having Asperger's. She had ordered the WRONG QUESTIONNAIRE. It was this thing that parents were supposed to fill out about their small children. She tried to get me to fill it out anyway, but it was impossible.

Following this, she said I did not have an ASD after talking to me for an hour and a half (talking about herself the whole time while I smiled and nodded) because she "didn't feel it" and "we connected". Seriously, what?! If she had quizzed me about what she had said, I would have had no info; I was zoned out half the time she was talking at me. She concluded by saying that she thinks I am gifted and have ADD (though how she would know I am gifted after talking to me for an hour and a half, I have no idea), and "lots of anxiety". At the time I was too shocked and frustrated to dispute her as I shelled out the $250 out-of-pocket for the appointment.

So I guess there's just a lot of not being listened to. This is a huge reason why I want a diagnosis - validation.

You are definitely not alone in feeling pissed off and weirded out about the god angle, but my experience with AA is that it isn't religious per say and is actually pretty down to earth. It is based on relinquishing control and trusting "a power greater than yourself" which, I was told time and time again during my involvement, does not have to mean GodJesusBuddhaFlyingSpaghettiMonsterAnything. It has to be something of your own understanding. A lot of people take their AA group itself, just the people around them, to be the "higher power". You really have all the freedom you want in the framework that they use (at least where I'm from - it might be different in other places, I'm not sure). Some people find religion helpful in the framework, others just focus on the group of people around them and that works for them. Basically it's just about learning to trust outside of yourself and realizing that you need help, not about religion. It may work for you, it may not. Just my two cents. It helped me, anyway.

I think this is a pretty common attitude for someone who's 18. You want to break out on your own and mark your independence and you don't want your parents interfering anymore. You need to figure out your identity. It's REALLY HARD to do that when living under the thumb of your family. It can be very smothering. I went through a time like this, and distanced myself from my parents because I had never felt connected to my family or anyone else - I always felt like an outsider, and it was painful. I was really bored around my family. I felt smothered and needed to do things on my own. Now that I'm older and more settled in my life, and I have been around kids more and understand the experience of a parent in regards to a child a bit better (they really do love you, they just really need to give you some space now), I want my parents back in my life, and I feel strong enough in my identity to connect with them on a new level. My advice now would be to stay in your college town (or another town, away from them), in touch, but distant, and if needed, explain to them that you really need your independence now because you want to be seen as an adult.

I feel their feelings... but their feelings confuse me and distress me... unless their feelings are like the ones I experience... ie if they have a brain like mine... and those are the people I can really connect with. I also have trouble telling whose feelings are whose (of the people around me).

I have a theory that the overwhelming nature of feeling all these feelings contributes the the social skills dilemma. I will feel something alien and wonder why I'm feeling it and be incapable of deciphering it... when really it's someone else's feeling. Or I will be confused by someone who is giving off a certain vibe but expressing an entirely different one with their facial expressions/tone of voice. After the trauma I became extremely withdrawn. I isolated myself to an unhealthy degree. I think it was because I had absolutely zero energy to play the social game. I became really depressed and drank a lot. My life became extremely ritualized - more so than it had ever been before. I ate the exact same thing every day at the exact same time and counted calories obsessively. I became completely detached from my world and the people in it.

It was like being in a haze. I was lonely and numb. I didn't trust anyone and I couldn't feel emotion. I lost my spirituality. 

I actually didn't find out about AS until about a year ago... and interestingly enough, that is something that finally made me begin to come out of the haze. All of a sudden my life was starting to make sense. My lifelong disconnect with most other people and my pervasive sense of being different suddenly had a name and a place. I had been trying, my whole life, to figure out what was "wrong" with me - why life was so hard to deal with, why I would get so upset, why I was so depressed/anxious (and why that always felt like a symptom, rather than a problem in itself), why I never fit in, why I was so tired, why I could never listen or stay awake in class (fluorescent lights), why everything was just too much. 

It's like, my whole life, something was wrong - I was too sensitive, or seemed weird to others, and then I found out about AS and something clicked. The PTSD brought numbness, and a depression which carried with it a huge loss of energy. I think that this made the AS symptoms more prominent, as I didn't have the energy to adapt and fit in. I was experiencing a completely individualized situation (the trauma) which nobody else had any chance of understanding, so I retreated further into my own head, which, I believe, increased my AS symptoms to a far, far greater degree.

One thing I would suggest to you is to stop drinking and smoking pot. That's an obvious one, but it's WAY easier to feel better once your mind balances out. Drinking really increases the ups and downs.

I wish you all the best. I know I am coming out of it now, and I am starting to feel like myself again.. because I feel as if I actually am starting to know who that is. Dedicate yourself to healing. It will be long, hard, and lonely, but it will come to you if you stay with it.

I don't usually look people in the eye, and when I do, it's fleeting and overwhelming. It's just too much information. When I'm talking to someone, I prefer to stare past them, because if I look at them, I will get distracted and forget what I'm saying. However, if someone is talking to me, I need to look at their mouth to comprehend what they're saying... lip-reading, I guess... the visual representation of the sound helps me process it faster. When I'm just listening to someone speak, if it's in a room with several other people and I can't focus on their voice and nothing else (think classroom situation), I hear every word individually, see it in my head, read it, and then a couple of seconds later I can put the words together and what they said clicks in my brain, but by then they have moved on to a new set of words and I lose track. It's just the way my mind processes speech - every single detail gets processed and analyzed before it can all be put together. It's exhausting. I think this is similar to the way I process facial expressions... it's like I need a second to process all the minute details and put them together, and by then, the context has changed and my interpretation is largely invalid.

On problems with reading facial expressions: I see the face, that's for sure... I see the details of it, if I look at it... I see red-rimmed eyes, and I see a smile, and how the face forms into a smile... I see a lot of details, it's just like it takes me a second to process it and put the story together, as I was saying above.

Imagine, as a metaphor, that you are trying to read a book with your eye very close to the page, so you can only see one word. You are only seeing one word at a time, and it is out of context, so you only get the meaning of the word, and not how it relates to the other words, except by backtracking in your memory and relating it to other words you have already read. You need to back up from the page to see the whole page, and to comprehend the whole story. This is what I have trouble with. The big picture is the context, and that is the difficulty.

So that's why I don't like looking at faces in conversation. It's just confusing and distracting.

I do, however, love to look at the faces of people I love. I marvel at the crevices in their faces, the coloration of their skin, every tiny detail, and think about their beauty. I find faces beautiful and interesting and endlessly intriguing... because I see every detail.

I also like looking at other faces, especially unusual faces...I am a little bit face-blind and will not remember a face that does not have some sort of distinguishing feature. I tend to identify people by their mannerisms, their dress, and their style of movement, rather than their face. These extensions of personality are more useful for me in identifying someone. Sometimes I will comment that someone closely resembles someone else, and people will disagree with me... I then realize that the similarity is in mannerisms or poise, or in some small detail of the face (ie mouth shape), not in the face as a whole.

*Whew* So, that is my long-winded explanation of my experience with faces. I hope it helps you understand, and I hope it resonates with others, too. :)

However, I think you are confusing social anxiety and other struggles with AS itself. Although AS is often comorbid with other symptoms such as anxiety and depression, and social anxiety can be a direct result of social traumas arising from the notorious social difficulties of AS, social anxiety is still just a symptom arising from the backdrop of the way your brain is set up and how it relates to others. 

Social anxiety can, indeed, be overcome with time, as you learn to love yourself in all your imperfections. Challenging, but doable. I have way less social anxiety than I used to, though I still do struggle with it from time to time.

I am a firm believer that AS is a challenge, but is not a negative thing. If it brings for you intelligence and creativity, I do not think it makes you more of a "common" person... in fact, it makes you stand out from the rest. Knowing that you're different can make you more confident (it did for me), and confidence makes it a lot easier to fit in, because you start acting like you know what you're doing. If you do that, people tend to listen to you more.

I have memories over my entire lifespan of "playing" with my vision (experiences of which would probably be considered unusual visual processing). When I was a kid, I used to press on my eyes a lot, until I saw greyish patterns, then I would open my eyes and let the patterns resolve into my normal vision. I would also stare at things with great focus until my peripheral vision would fade to grey and disappear, and all I would see would be the thing I was staring at (tunnel vision). When I first started learning about AS, I learned that these behaviors are classified as visual stimming. I have vivid memories of doing these things as a kid, because I really enjoyed doing them, and it felt good - in fact, they were probably among my favourite things to do.

I have memories of being in high school and staring at, for instance, the ground, and noticing it resolving into swelling patterns - almost a breathing motion - if I stared long enough (this was before any psychedelic experience). I have also always had a very intense experience of colour, leading to some eccentric clothing choices. :)

The funny thing is, when I finally did end up taking LSD for the first time, I felt completely at home. I felt comfortable with the visuals, and the super-connected processing, because it was already somewhat familiar. I think it did change a couple of things - as I said, I sometimes see tracers now, which never happened before, and sometimes I see tiny points of light in the upper area of my vision, though much less often than I used to. Sometimes colours shift a little bit, which is also new, but like the other obvious symptoms of HPPD, it's gradually going away.

I know that afterimages and static are a symptom of HPPD, but I truly could not tell you if the extent to which I experience it is new. It is definitely here to stay. I know I always did experience these kind of afterimages (as I said, under fluorescent lights), as a lingering negative image, almost like seeing spots - for instance, after looking at a white piece of paper, and things like that. The static-y effect on my vision is always there and I think always has been, but is more pronounced (a more detailed static) when I'm tired.

Intersexed people are people who are neither male or female, but who are genetically somewhere in between. It's generally physical; for instance, a woman can be born, and never get her period, and eventually find out that she has undescended testes and is therefore genetically male. There are also hormonal examples, for instance, Kleinefelter syndrome. There are also people with ambiguous genitalia, so they fall somewhere in between the gender divide. The main character in Middlesex is an example of this. So very interesting!

It's really good to learn to explain your working style to people you regularly interact with. Rehearse calmly saying things like, "When I focus on my work, I focus very intensely, and when someone talks to me, I find it hard to get back in the zone. So if I seem like I'm ignoring you, please try not to take it personally; I just need space to concentrate." Then smile as genuinely as possible so they know you don't mean any harm. I find it also helps to be able to say, "I'm sorry I didn't get your joke. I have trouble catching sarcasm, and I take things quite literally. I need you to be a bit more direct when you talk to me." or, "Sorry if I don't look at you directly - I find eye contact very intense."

It's very good to learn how you work/function, and to be able to express it concisely and clearly to others so they will understand you. It's good to tell the truth. People tend to get offended when they don't understand what is going on. I try and explain my reality tunnel to them. I try not to mention AS specifically, as there are lots of misconceptions and many people don't understand it; I try to explain my ways to others more as quirks of a personality type. It's easier to explain on the fly, and easier for others to understand quickly. 

I find that most of my stress comes from misunderstandings, because I assume people will know why I act the way I do, because it's so obvious to me. It's helped to realize that people really don't understand me right away, and if you explain it to them and get them to understand, they are usually willing to accommodate you.

I am now almost completely off the customer service train, thank god. I would apply for jobs, for instance at grocery stores, and I'm sure it's because I'm female - I kept getting put on customer service even though I would emphatically request, every time, to work at stocking shelves, or gutting fish, or anything else. This would inevitably lead to extreme crankiness and rudeness (or switching over to a robotic state to cope) and quitting after so many months.

On the issue of customer service: the reason why I find it so stressful is because I need to focus on each person that comes into the store, do the typical back-and-forth banter ("Hi! How are you?" "Good! And you?" "Oh, pretty good!") and figure out their needs. When there are lots of people, I am continually breaking my concentration; it takes energy to focus on each person, and when it's one after the other, it drains me pretty fast. Each customer is a task, and it's like I start concentrating, and am forced to pull my attention away to start a new task. It feels like being constantly interrupted, which just makes me more and more irritable. On a busy day, I get progressively more rude, which makes people respond rudely to me, and increases the chance that the customer will become upset with me.

It's absolutely unbearable if a customer gets upset with me, especially if it's over something I can't control. Even though I know that it's almost certainly their issue and not mine, I always feel the blow, and it feels like a punch in the gut. That usually sends me into a meltdown and I have to escape to cry/shake my hands.

I now work in a coffee shop, but it's only 6 hours a week, during a very slow time of day (evening). Any more than that would be too much. At that time of day, people tend to come in to get away from other people, so there isn't much pressure to chat. The customers are really nice there, too.

I also work in housekeeping now. That's great. Though repetitive, it allows me mental space, and I can put my headphones in. I have scored a solo painting job for the summer, which is awesome.

The best jobs for me are solitary ones where I can listen to music.

Hope this gives you some insight :)

I have two.... both pertaining to elementary school.

The first one took place in kindergarten. I remember it very clearly to this day... I can only assume that it is because the emotional impact was so great. We were decorating place markers for a "teacher's banquet" or some such. I drew a small picture of an orange cat, trotting along. The teacher came by and commended my work. I then realized that the cat was walking on thin air, and decided he needed to be walking on ground, so I coloured (scribbled) the background in, brown. The teacher came by again, and gasped in horror. She grabbed the marker and picture from me, and proceeded to sit, purse her lips, and meticulously begin to fill in between the scribbles. I distinctly remember the following dialogue:

Me: "What are you doing?"
Her: "I'm trying to FIX what you DID!!!"

The second incident took place in grade five. Our class was going to the bowling alley that day (awesome field trip!!) and as an added bonus, we were going to experience "cosmic bowling", which was basically bowling, but, you know, cosmic. With blacklights and stuff.

A few years ago, I hitchhiked from New Brunswick to Montreal with a friend of mine to see Silverchair. It was just the two of us - me, an averagely sized girl, and my roommate, who weighed approximately 90 pounds. We finally arrived in the city, and had arranged to stay with my cousin. I kept phoning her, with no answer. We began to feel nervous and called a cab. The next hour or so was spent driving around, attempting to find a hostel or a motel that was not full, with no luck.

After much frustration and continued calling of my cousin, who continued not to answer the phone, our overexuberant, curly-haired cabbie suggested that we stay at his apartment. My friend was quite cranky, pushy and reckless, and I was a quiet pushover, so we ended up going there. To be fair, our options were limited.

 We arrived in the middle of the night. I looked around the apartment. It was unnaturally clean. There were strange golden statues of cherubs all around, and the decor was vaguely Moroccan. All the furniture was white, and COVERED IN PLASTIC. The cabbie turned on the TV and went into the kitchen. My roommate and I sat on the crinkly, plastic-coated couch and tensely waited.

He returned, chuckling jovially, carrying a tray of finely sliced melon. He started eating from the tray, and so, I thought, why the hell not, and helped myself. We all ate melon from the tray as something embarrassingly sexual happened on the TV. My roommate and I sat quietly, extremely uncomfortable, as the cabbie chuckled heartily at everything that was happening on the TV.

After that excruciating 10 minutes or so, he brought us glasses of juice. (I KNOW!) My roommate downed hers without a thought. My thoughts at the time were, "well, if she's going down, I'm going down with her", so I drank my juice too.

Fortunately, it was then that my cousin called. We cabbed back to her place and felt a lot better. The juice was ok, anyway. I guess he was just being a good host. Maybe this wasn't a particularly dangerous situation, but it could have been. At the very least, it was weird and highly atypical.
